marble.name: Newton's Third Law
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: State and apply Newton's Third Law: every force has an equal and opposite reaction force acting on a different object, distinguishing action-reaction pairs from balanced forces
marble.prompt: If you saw a video of a rocket launching into space, could they explain what force is pushing the rocket upward and where that force comes from — and which law of motion that demonstrates?

cluster.summary: Your child is learning about forces — understanding how pushes and pulls can make objects move faster, slower, or change direction, and testing different ways to affect motion.

misconceptions: Pairing the two forces on the SAME body and concluding they cancel — conflating a third-law pair with balanced forces (the central error; Taber)
During acceleration the 'active' pusher exerts the bigger force ('Blue pushes Green harder to start the motion') — reported in ~100% of incoming students and very stubborn
The more massive object exerts more force (forces are equal; different EFFECTS come from different masses)
'Action' then 'reaction' implies a time sequence (B responds after A), rather than simultaneous forces
Third-law forces 'cancel out' (they act on different bodies, so can never cancel on one body)
representations: Two separate free-body diagrams side by side, one per body, each showing its half of the pair on a different object
The 'swap and reverse' test (A↔B) to locate the partner force
Book / table / Earth three-bodies diagram separating the interaction pairs from the balanced forces on the book
authoredAnswer: The first student is right. A Third Law pair is two forces of the SAME type acting on DIFFERENT objects: the table pushes up on the book and the book pushes down on the table. The book's weight (Earth pulling the book) acts on the SAME object as the table's push — the book — so those two are BALANCED forces, not a pair; weight's actual pair is the book pulling the Earth up. To find a pair: state 'A acts on B', and it
probe: Hook two identical newton-meters (or force sensors) together and have two students pull — one gently, one hard. Ask the class to predict what each meter reads, and WHY, before they pull. Predicting the 'stronger' puller's meter reads more reveals the unequal-force idea; both reading the same, even during acceleration o

wrongAnswers.wrong: Yes — the table's push up and the book's weight are the Third Law pair, equal and opposite.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Identifies two forces acting on the SAME object (the book) as a Third Law pair.
wrongAnswers.fix: Insist on naming both objects for every force; a pair must act on two different objects, so weight and the table's push (both on the book) are balanced, not a pair.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Describes a sequence, a delay, or a 'winner' between the two forces.
wrongAnswers.fix: Drop 'action/reaction' language: 'if A pushes B, B pushes A back equally AT THE SAME TIME' — the two forces are simultaneous.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Says the forces in a collision are unequal (the bigger object wins).
wrongAnswers.fix: The pair is always equal even for very different masses; the different DAMAGE comes from different accelerations (F = ma), not different forces.

before.name: Newton's First & Second Laws
before.reason: Newton's Third Law is conventionally taught after the first two — students need Newton's 1st and 2nd as reference points to distinguish reaction pairs from balanced forces
